summary: Bio-Orbit is a satellite-based decision-support platform designed to help small-scale potato farmers in Ecuador's Andean highlands make better agricultural decisions. It integrates five years of NASA POWER climate data with Sentinel-2 satellite imagery to monitor weather conditions, soil moisture, vegetation health, and crop stress. By combining regional climate risks with field-level observations, the platform generates localized alerts for frost, drought, irrigation needs, heat stress, and potential late blight outbreaks. It also provides practical recommendations with AI-powered conversational assistant to support crop rotation planning. Bio-Orbit addresses the challenge of limited access to agricultural information by transforming open satellite observations into actionable insights through an accessible web application, without requiring expensive sensors or additional hardware. This project is important because it empowers smallholder farmers to anticipate risks, reduce crop losses, optimize water and agrochemical use, and improve long-term soil health, contributing to more resilient and sustainable agriculture in the Andean region.
details:
Demo: https://bio-orbit.elpitagoras14.qzz.io/

What does it do and how does it work?

Bio-Orbit is a decision-support tool for small potato farmers in Ecuador's Andean highlands. Our pilot plot is a 1.17-hectare potato field in Toacaso / Sigchos (Cotopaxi), at 3,588 m above sea level. It combines two NASA-related Earth observation sources and turns them into plain-language advice a farmer can act on.

  1. Locate the plot. The farmer opens the web app on a phone, finds their field with GPS and draws its outline on a map.
  2. Read the regional climate (NASA POWER). We process five years of daily NASA POWER data: temperature, rainfall, relative humidity, root-zone and surface soil moisture, and evapotranspiration. A weekly agroclimatic model produces traffic-light indicators for frost, irrigation need and heat stress. It also gives a 30-day outlook with preventive alerts for late blight ("lancha"), drought, nutrient leaching and frost.
  3. Watch the plot itself (Sentinel-2). We pull Sentinel-2 L2A imagery at 10 m resolution from the open STAC catalog on AWS. We keep only the scenes that are cloud-free over the plot, about one every 15 days. Then we compute NDVI (vigor), NDRE (chlorophyll and nitrogen) and NDMI (leaf water) pixel by pixel. Each part of the field is classified as healthy, watch or critical, broken down by sector (N/S/E/W).
  4. Cross-check the two sources. This is the core idea. NASA POWER says whether there is a risk, and Sentinel-2 confirms whether there is already visible damage. When both agree, the alert becomes confirmed. One example is "weather favors late blight and vigor dropped in the north sector: apply preventive control today." When they disagree, the farmer is told to inspect the field. Each satellite image is compared with the weather of that same week, not today's.
  5. Plan the next crop. A conversational agent helps inexperienced farmers choose what to plant after (or before) potato. It draws on a knowledge base of Andean crop rotations taken from FAO and MAGAP sources.

What benefits does it have?

  • Early, specific warnings. A farmer can treat one sector of the field before a problem spreads, instead of spraying everything or reacting too late.
  • Fewer false alarms. Alerts are confirmed by two independent data sources.
  • Advice in plain Spanish. It says what to do this week (irrigate, open drainage channels, apply foliar fertilizer, check the lower leaves) and doesn't just show charts.
  • No extra cost to the farmer. NASA POWER, Sentinel-2 and Open-Meteo data are all free and open, and no sensors or hardware are needed in the field.
  • Healthier soil over time. Rotation planning breaks the pest and disease cycles that build up when potato is planted again and again.

What is the intended impact?

Potato is a staple crop and the main source of income for many Andean families. Yet most smallholders make decisions without data, and they lose harvests to frost, late blight, drought and waterlogging. We want satellite data that normally only researchers and large farms use to reach a farmer with a phone. The goals are less crop loss, more efficient use of water and agrochemicals, and stronger long-term soil health through better rotations.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data sources:
    • NASA POWER API (daily agroclimatology)
    • Copernicus Sentinel-2 L2A through the Earth Search STAC catalog on AWS
    • Open-Meteo / ERA5, used to calibrate temperature for altitude
    • Retrieval: a hybrid search that combines keyword search (BM25) and vector search on SQLite (sqlite-vec).
    • Recommendations: a deterministic rules engine produces them. The language model only talks with the farmer and explains; it never does the calculations.
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite and Leaflet (with leaflet-draw) for mobile-first maps, plot drawing and GPS location.
  • Deployment: Docker and Docker Compose, deployed with Dokploy.
  • Hardware: none in the field. A phone and an internet connection are enough.

How is the project creative?

  • Two scales, one answer. NASA POWER describes a grid cell of about 50 km, while Sentinel-2 sees 10 m pixels. Instead of choosing one, we use each for what it does best: climate risk and observed damage. The cross-check gives an alert that neither source could give alone.
  • Altitude correction. NASA POWER places our plot at the average height of its grid cell, about 2,500 m, while the real field is at 3,588 m. At that gap, uncorrected temperatures would never trigger a frost alert. We measured the bias against Open-Meteo over 1,690 shared days (about −7 °C). It matches the theoretical lapse rate (6.5 °C per km), and we apply it only to the frost and heat rules.
  • An AI that explains but doesn't invent. The agent's recommendations come from a transparent, testable rules engine and from cited agronomic sources, not from free-form text generated by the model.

What factors did the team consider?

  1. The user. Farmers with little technical experience who speak Spanish and use a phone, so the app needs simple screens, trafficlight colors and concrete actions.
  2. Andean clouds. Many Sentinel-2 passes are cloudy, so we filter clouds over the plot polygon itself and keep the last valid image.
  3. Data limits, stated openly. Regional climate data doesn't fully represent a 1-hectare field. Every alert therefore says which source supports it, and mismatches are flagged for a field check rather than hidden.
  4. Agronomic grounding. Thresholds and rotations come from FAO and MAGAP sources, and the knowledge base is focused on potato and the rotations that include it.
  5. Cost and openness. Only free, open data is used, so the solution can scale to other plots and regions.
  6. Privacy. The agent keeps only short-term memory per session and stores nothing between sessions.
